To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
catecholamines increase virulence in Vibrio anguilliarm and Vibrio campbellei, and that this is due to catecholamine-induced growth in media containing blood.
catecholamines (norepinephrine and/or dopamine) increase virulence in pathogenic vibrios, and that this effect can be partially blocked by catecholamine antagonists.
the catecholamine dopamine and the catecholaminergic receptor antagonist phentolamine increase the virulence toward freshwater prawn larvae of pathogenic vibrio bacteria that infect aquatic animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that the stress hormones norephinephrine and dopamine play in the pathogenicity of Vibrio species.
the role of the catechols norepinephrin and dopamine in the pathogenesis of the fish pathogen Vibrio anguilarum.
the impact of stress hormones on bacterial virulence and the development of novel antibacterial agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
catecholamines are important for vibrios, but the precise mechanisms involved are still unknown.
catecholamines can increase virulence of vibrio pathogens by increasing motility, growth and survival in serum containing media.
catecholamines are virulence factors for vibrios.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
catecholamines are stressors for pathogenic vibrios and that the virulence of these pathogens is enhanced by catecholamines in the aquatic environment.
catecholamine-stimulated vibrio virulence is mediated by catecholamine binding to eukaryotic receptors, and that this binding results in the release of a bacterial virulence factor.

catecholamines increase the virulence in a dose-dependent manner by inducing motility and growth of the pathogenic vibrios, and that this effect is mediated by catecholamine binding to specific receptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
catecholamines may play a role in bacterial infections and that antagonists may be useful in reducing bacterial infections.
catecholamines can be used as a tool to enhance the virulence of bacteria that are pathogenic for fish and crustaceans.
stress hormones can be used to increase virulence in vibrios and other pathogens that infect aquatic organisms.
